concepts.title: How to palpate
concepts.body: Explain, gain consent and expose only what you need (offer a chaperone). Use **flat finger pads**, start **light then deeper**, move slowly and **compare with the other side**.
bullets: Watch the patient's face for pain
concepts.ur: Ijazat lein, sirf zaroori hissa kholen, ungliyon ke pad se pehle halka phir gehra dabayen aur dono sides compare karein.

concepts.title: Landmarks that mark spinal levels
concepts.body: Use several landmarks together — each one alone is often a level out.

concepts.title: Palpate layer by layer
concepts.body: Feel each layer in turn: **skin** (temperature, moisture, swelling), **subcutaneous tissue** (oedema — does it pit?), **muscle** (tone, tenderness, trigger points), **tendon and ligament** (thickening, tenderness), then **bone** (contour, steps, bony tenderness).

concepts.title: Peripheral pulses

head: Pulse
Where
rows: Lateral wrist, beside the radial styloid
Medial to the biceps tendon at the elbow crease
Deep in the popliteal fossa, knee slightly bent
Lateral to the EHL tendon on the foot

concepts.body: Check pulses before compression, after trauma, and in anyone with claudication or diabetes.

concepts.title: What tenderness means
concepts.body: Many structures are **normally tender** (coracoid, lateral epicondyle region, trigger points). Tenderness matters when it is **one-sided**, **reproduces the familiar pain**, or is **bony tenderness after trauma**. Palpation adds to — never replaces — history and movement testing.

concepts.title: Palpation is less precise than we think
concepts.body: Identifying a single spinal level by palpation is often out by one level, and agreement between clinicians on 'stiffness' is low. Combine landmarks, re-check with movement, and document what you felt rather than over-interpreting it.

concepts.title: Ottawa rules: palpation that decides X-rays
bullets: Ankle X-ray: bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus (distal 6 cm), or unable to bear weight 4 steps
Foot X-ray: tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal or the navicular, or unable to bear weight
Knee X-ray: age 55+, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, cannot flex to 90°, or cannot bear weight
concepts.body: After acute injury these rules use palpation to decide who needs imaging:

concepts.title: Findings to act on
bullets: Hot, red, swollen joint with fever — septic arthritis until proven otherwise
Pulsatile, expanding abdominal mass — abdominal aortic aneurysm
Swollen, tender calf after surgery or immobility — DVT
Hard, fixed, painless lump or enlarged lymph nodes — refer
Cold, pale limb with absent pulses — acute ischaemia

questions.prompt: Before palpating you should…
options: Explain, gain consent and offer a chaperone
Palpate through thick clothing
Only palpate the painful side
Start pressing firmly at once
questions.explain: Consent and dignity first.

questions.prompt: The top of the iliac crests is level with…
options: L1
L4
S2

questions.prompt: The inferior angle of the scapula is level with…
options: C7
T3
T7

questions.prompt: Why compare with the other side?
options: It is faster
To warm your hands
Only for children
To tell normal tenderness and shape from abnormal
questions.explain: The other side is the patient's own normal.

questions.prompt: How do you tell C7 from C6?
options: C7 is always smaller
Rotate the trunk
Flex the neck fully
Extend the neck — C6 slides forward and disappears, C7 stays
questions.explain: C7 is the vertebra prominens.

questions.prompt: Which structure in the popliteal fossa is deepest?
options: Popliteal vein
Tibial nerve
Popliteal artery
Small saphenous vein
questions.explain: Nerve superficial, vein, artery deepest.

questions.prompt: The ischial tuberosity is easiest to palpate with the patient…
options: Sitting
Side-lying with the hip flexed
Standing upright
Prone with the hip extended
questions.explain: Hip flexion moves gluteus maximus off it.

questions.prompt: From lateral to medial in the femoral triangle:
options: Artery, nerve, vein
Nerve, vein, artery
Nerve, artery, vein
Vein, artery, nerve
questions.explain: NAV(Y) from lateral to medial.

questions.prompt: Foot drop after a tight below-knee cast suggests compression at…
options: The tibial tuberosity
The popliteal artery
The medial malleolus
The neck of the fibula
questions.explain: The common fibular nerve winds around the fibular neck.

questions.prompt: A 13-year-old footballer with a tender, bony lump on the tibial tuberosity most likely has…
options: Osgood–Schlatter disease
Patellar tendinopathy at the inferior pole
Prepatellar bursitis
Tibial fracture
questions.explain: Traction apophysitis at the tuberosity in adolescents.

questions.prompt: Lateral hip pain with tenderness over the greater trochanter, worse lying on that side, suggests…
options: Hip OA only
Meralgia paraesthetica
Gluteal tendinopathy (greater trochanteric pain syndrome)
Sacroiliac joint pain
questions.explain: Classic GTPS presentation.

questions.prompt: Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after a fall on an outstretched hand suggests…
options: Wrist sprain only
Carpal tunnel syndrome
Scaphoid fracture — immobilise and image
De Quervain's tenosynovitis
questions.explain: Snuffbox tenderness = scaphoid until proven otherwise.

questions.case: Inversion ankle injury: tender at the tip of the lateral malleolus; walked 4 steps with a limp.
questions.prompt: X-ray needed (Ottawa)?
options: No — walking 4 steps excludes fracture
No — ankle X-rays are never needed
Only if swelling persists for 6 weeks
Yes — bone tenderness at the malleolar tip
questions.explain: Malleolar bone tenderness alone meets the rule.

questions.case: A 70-year-old with back pain: you feel a pulsatile, expanding mass above the umbilicus.
questions.prompt: Action?
options: Urgent medical referral — suspected abdominal aortic aneurysm
Lumbar mobilisation
Soft-tissue massage
Core strengthening
questions.explain: Expansile pulsation = AAA red flag.

questions.case: Hot, red, swollen knee, temperature 38.6 °C, can't bear weight; no injury.
questions.prompt: Most urgent concern?
options: Osteoarthritis flare
Septic arthritis — same-day medical referral
Baker's cyst
Patellar tendinopathy
questions.explain: Hot joint + fever = septic arthritis until proven otherwise.

questions.case: Neck examination: you count down from C7 and mark 'T6' — your colleague finds T7 on the same patient.
questions.prompt: Best interpretation?
options: The patient has an extra vertebra
Palpation is useless
Palpation of a single spinal level is often one level out — combine landmarks and document
One of you is incompetent
questions.explain: Known limitation; use multiple landmarks and movement.

questions.case: Diabetes: dorsalis pedis not felt on either foot; posterior tibial pulses present.
questions.prompt: Interpretation?
options: Normal — no further checks
DVT
Definite arterial occlusion — emergency
Can be a normal anatomical variant — but check ABPI given the diabetes
questions.explain: DP can be congenitally absent; diabetes warrants objective testing.

questions.case: Knee injury: 60-year-old, tender only over the patella, can bend to 100°, walked into clinic.
questions.prompt: X-ray (Ottawa knee)?
options: Yes — age 55+ and isolated patellar tenderness both meet the rule
No — flexes past 90°
No — able to walk
Only an MRI
questions.explain: Any single criterion triggers imaging.

questions.case: Pain at the medial elbow when gripping; positive Tinel's sign behind the medial epicondyle with tingling into the little finger.
questions.prompt: Which structures are involved?
options: Radial nerve and extensor origin
Biceps tendon
Common flexor origin and possibly the ulnar nerve in the cubital tunnel
Median nerve in the carpal tunnel
questions.explain: Medial epicondylalgia can co-exist with ulnar neuropathy.

questions.case: Behind-knee swelling with calf tightness after a long flight; calf 3.5 cm larger.
questions.prompt: Before calling it a Baker's cyst you must…
options: Massage it
Start resisted knee flexion
Rule out DVT — refer for assessment
Aspirate it yourself
questions.explain: Calf swelling after immobility = DVT risk.

questions.case: Insertional heel pain right at the bone, worse with uphill walking; tender at the Achilles insertion, not 4 cm above.
questions.prompt: Implication for loading?
options: Mid-portion tendinopathy — start eccentric heel drops below step level
Calcaneal fracture
Plantar fasciitis
Insertional tendinopathy — avoid dorsiflexion compression early (e.g. heel drops off a step)
questions.explain: Insertional tendons are compressed in dorsiflexion; load flat first.

questions.prompt: Which finding makes tenderness most clinically meaningful?
options: Tenderness in a trigger point on both sides
It reproduces the patient's familiar pain and differs from the other side
Any tenderness at all
Tenderness over the coracoid
questions.explain: Familiar, asymmetric pain — not tenderness alone.

stations.title: Palpate the shoulder girdle
stations.scenario: A 30-year-old fell onto the right shoulder. Palpate and identify the key landmarks.
tasks: Palpate from the sternoclavicular joint along the clavicle.
Identify the AC joint, acromion and coracoid.
checklist: Explains, gains consent and exposes appropriately
Palpates with flat finger pads, light to deep
Follows the clavicle to the AC joint and notes any step
Finds the coracoid in the deltopectoral groove
Links a stepped, tender AC joint with AC separation

stations.title: Find the spinal levels
stations.scenario: Mark C7, T3, T7, L4 and S2 on a standing model using surface landmarks.
tasks: Identify each level using at least one landmark.
checklist: Confirms C7 with the C6 extension test
Uses the scapular spine root for T3 and the inferior angle for T7
Uses the iliac crest tops for L4
Uses the PSIS dimples for S2
States that single-level palpation is often one level out

stations.title: Acute ankle: palpate and apply the Ottawa rules
stations.scenario: A 22-year-old inverted the ankle playing basketball an hour ago. Palpate and decide on imaging.
tasks: Palpate the malleoli (posterior edge and tip, distal 6 cm).
Palpate the base of the 5th metatarsal and the navicular.
Check weight bearing and decide on X-ray.
checklist: Palpates the posterior edge and tip of both malleoli
Palpates the base of the 5th metatarsal and the navicular
Palpates the ATFL separately from bone
Asks the patient to take 4 steps
Explains the decision to the patient

cards.front: Where do you find the Suprasternal (jugular) notch?
cards.back: Top of the sternum, between the inner ends of the clavicles

cards.front: How do you palpate the Suprasternal (jugular) notch?
cards.back: Slide a finger down the front of the neck until it drops into the dip above the sternum

cards.front: What is the Suprasternal (jugular) notch a landmark for?
cards.back: T2 vertebral level; starting point for counting down the sternum

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Suprasternal (jugular) notch?
cards.back: Trachea centrally above it; sternoclavicular joints on each side

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Suprasternal (jugular) notch?
cards.back: Check the trachea is central — it deviates in tension pneumothorax or lung collapse

cards.front: Where do you find the Sternal angle (angle of Louis)?
cards.back: Horizontal ridge about 5 cm below the suprasternal notch, where the manubrium meets the sternal body

cards.front: How do you palpate the Sternal angle (angle of Louis)?
cards.back: From the notch, slide down the sternum until you feel a transverse bony ridge

cards.front: What is the Sternal angle (angle of Louis) a landmark for?
cards.back: 2nd costal cartilage (count ribs from here); T4–T5 level

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Sternal angle (angle of Louis)?
cards.back: 2nd costal cartilages; the tracheal bifurcation and aortic arch lie at this level

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Sternal angle (angle of Louis)?
cards.back: Reliable start for counting ribs and intercostal spaces (auscultation, chest expansion)

cards.front: Where do you find the Xiphoid process?
cards.back: Lower tip of the sternum, where the two costal margins meet

cards.front: How do you palpate the Xiphoid process?
cards.back: Follow the sternum down to the small pointed end at the top of the upper abdomen

cards.front: What is the Xiphoid process a landmark for?
cards.back: T9 level; lower point for chest-expansion measurement

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Xiphoid process?
cards.back: Costal margins, linea alba; the liver lies to the right

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Xiphoid process?
cards.back: CPR compressions go on the lower half of the sternum — not on the xiphoid

cards.front: Where do you find the Acromioclavicular (AC) joint?
cards.back: Top of the shoulder, where the outer end of the clavicle meets the acromion

cards.front: How do you palpate the Acromioclavicular (AC) joint?
cards.back: Follow the clavicle outwards until you feel a small step or dip just before the acromion

cards.front: What is the Acromioclavicular (AC) joint a landmark for?
cards.back: Lateral end of the clavicle; joint line for AC tests

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Acromioclavicular (AC) joint?
cards.back: Acromion, coracoclavicular ligaments, supraspinatus tendon beneath

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Acromioclavicular (AC) joint?
cards.back: Tender and stepped after AC separation (fall onto the shoulder); painful cross-body adduction

cards.front: Where do you find the Coracoid process?
cards.back: Below the outer third of the clavicle, deep in the deltopectoral groove

cards.front: How do you palpate the Coracoid process?
cards.back: Press deeply in the deltopectoral groove 2–3 cm below the clavicle for a tender bony knob

cards.front: What is the Coracoid process a landmark for?
cards.back: Attachment of pectoralis minor, short head of biceps and coracobrachialis

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Coracoid process?
cards.back: Brachial plexus and axillary vessels pass just medial to it

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Coracoid process?
cards.back: Often tender even when healthy — compare sides; landmark for anterior shoulder injections

cards.front: Where do you find the Medial epicondyle?
cards.back: Prominent bony point on the inner side of the elbow

cards.front: How do you palpate the Medial epicondyle?
cards.back: Elbow at 90°, feel the largest bony bump on the medial side

cards.front: What is the Medial epicondyle a landmark for?
cards.back: Common flexor origin (wrist and finger flexors, pronator teres)

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Medial epicondyle?
cards.back: Ulnar nerve in the groove behind it (cubital tunnel)

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Medial epicondyle?
cards.back: Tender in medial epicondylalgia ('golfer's elbow'); tap behind it for ulnar nerve Tinel's sign

cards.front: Where do you find the Lateral epicondyle?
cards.back: Bony point on the outer side of the elbow

cards.front: How do you palpate the Lateral epicondyle?
cards.back: Elbow at 90°, feel the bony bump on the lateral side just above the radial head

cards.front: What is the Lateral epicondyle a landmark for?
cards.back: Common extensor origin (ECRB); axis for elbow goniometry

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Lateral epicondyle?
cards.back: Radial head just below it — feel it turn during pronation and supination

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Lateral epicondyle?
cards.back: Tender just below and in front of it in lateral epicondylalgia ('tennis elbow')

cards.front: Where do you find the Radial styloid?
cards.back: Bony tip on the thumb side of the wrist

cards.front: How do you palpate the Radial styloid?
cards.back: Follow the radius down the thumb side of the forearm to the wrist

cards.front: What is the Radial styloid a landmark for?
cards.back: Distal point for forearm length; edge of the anatomical snuffbox

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Radial styloid?
cards.back: Anatomical snuffbox (scaphoid) and the APL/EPB tendons (first extensor compartment)

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Radial styloid?
cards.back: Tender here with a positive Finkelstein test = De Quervain's tenosynovitis

cards.front: Where do you find the Olecranon?
cards.back: The point of the elbow at the back

cards.front: How do you palpate the Olecranon?
cards.back: Bend the elbow and feel the prominent bony tip at the back

cards.front: What is the Olecranon a landmark for?
cards.back: Triceps insertion; forms a triangle with both epicondyles when the elbow is bent

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Olecranon?
cards.back: Olecranon bursa over it; ulnar nerve on its medial side

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Olecranon?
cards.back: A soft swelling over it = olecranon bursitis; the epicondyle triangle is disrupted in elbow dislocation

cards.front: Where do you find the C7 spinous process?
cards.back: The most prominent spinous process at the base of the neck

cards.front: How do you palpate the C7 spinous process?
cards.back: Extend the neck: C6 slides forward and disappears under your finger, C7 stays (vertebra prominens)

cards.front: What is the C7 spinous process a landmark for?
cards.back: Start for counting thoracic spinous processes; top point for posture photographs

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the C7 spinous process?
cards.back: T1 spinous process just below (also prominent)

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the C7 spinous process?
cards.back: Reference point for the craniovertebral angle and spinal measurements

cards.front: Where do you find the Spine of the scapula (root)?
cards.back: Bony ridge across the back of the scapula; its medial end is level with T3

cards.front: How do you palpate the Spine of the scapula (root)?
cards.back: Run your fingers medially across the upper scapula from the acromion

cards.front: What is the Spine of the scapula (root) a landmark for?
cards.back: T3 spinous process level

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Spine of the scapula (root)?
cards.back: Supraspinatus above it, infraspinatus below it

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Spine of the scapula (root)?
cards.back: Wasting above or below it suggests suprascapular nerve or rotator cuff problems

cards.front: Where do you find the Inferior angle of the scapula?
cards.back: Lowest point of the scapula, level with T7

cards.front: How do you palpate the Inferior angle of the scapula?
cards.back: Follow the medial border of the scapula down to its tip

cards.front: What is the Inferior angle of the scapula a landmark for?
cards.back: T7 spinous process level

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Inferior angle of the scapula?
cards.back: Latissimus dorsi crosses over it; serratus anterior attaches to its deep surface

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Inferior angle of the scapula?
cards.back: Watch it during arm elevation for winging and scapular dyskinesis

cards.front: Where do you find the Iliac crest (highest point)?
cards.back: Upper rim of the pelvis at the waist; the highest points are level with L4

cards.front: How do you palpate the Iliac crest (highest point)?
cards.back: Hands on the waist, press down onto the bony rim; a line joining both tops (Tuffier's line) crosses L4

cards.front: What is the Iliac crest (highest point) a landmark for?
cards.back: L4 spinous process / L4–L5 interspace

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Iliac crest (highest point)?
cards.back: Quadratus lumborum and erector spinae attach; cluneal nerves cross it

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Iliac crest (highest point)?
cards.back: Compare heights for pelvic tilt and leg-length difference; level used for lumbar puncture

cards.front: Where do you find the Posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS)?
cards.back: Bony points under the 'dimples of Venus' above the buttocks; level with S2

cards.front: How do you palpate the Posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS)?
cards.back: Find the skin dimples above the buttocks and press up and in with the thumbs

cards.front: What is the Posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) a landmark for?
cards.back: S2 level; the sacroiliac joint region

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS)?
cards.back: Sacroiliac joint just below and medial; long dorsal sacroiliac ligament

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS)?
cards.back: Compare heights in standing; landmark for sacroiliac tests and the Schober measure

cards.front: Where do you find the Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)?
cards.back: Front end of the iliac crest, at each side of the lower abdomen

cards.front: How do you palpate the Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)?
cards.back: Hands on the hips, slide the thumbs forward and down to the bony point at the front

cards.front: What is the Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) a landmark for?
cards.back: Origin of sartorius; start point for true leg length and the Q-angle

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)?
cards.back: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve passes just medial to it; the inguinal ligament attaches

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)?
cards.back: Compare heights for pelvic tilt; avulsion fractures in adolescent sprinters (sartorius)

cards.front: Where do you find the Femoral pulse (mid-inguinal point)?
cards.back: Halfway between the ASIS and the pubic symphysis, just below the inguinal ligament

cards.front: How do you palpate the Femoral pulse (mid-inguinal point)?
cards.back: Supine, hip slightly abducted and turned out; press firmly just below the middle of the groin crease

cards.front: What is the Femoral pulse (mid-inguinal point) a landmark for?
cards.back: The femoral triangle — nerve, artery, vein from lateral to medial (NAV)

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Femoral pulse (mid-inguinal point)?
cards.back: Femoral nerve lateral to it, femoral vein medial to it

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Femoral pulse (mid-inguinal point)?
cards.back: Weak or absent with peripheral arterial disease — check lower-limb circulation

cards.front: Where do you find the Greater trochanter?
cards.back: Bony prominence on the outer side of the upper thigh

cards.front: How do you palpate the Greater trochanter?
cards.back: Palpate the lateral hip below the iliac crest; it rolls under your hand as the hip rotates

cards.front: What is the Greater trochanter a landmark for?
cards.back: Axis for hip goniometry; plumb-line point on the side view

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Greater trochanter?
cards.back: Gluteus medius and minimus tendons insert here; trochanteric bursa

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Greater trochanter?
cards.back: Lateral hip tenderness here = greater trochanteric pain syndrome (gluteal tendinopathy)

cards.front: Where do you find the Ischial tuberosity?
cards.back: Bony point at the bottom of the buttock (the 'sitting bone')

cards.front: How do you palpate the Ischial tuberosity?
cards.back: Side-lying with the hip bent (moves gluteus maximus away), press up into the gluteal fold

cards.front: What is the Ischial tuberosity a landmark for?
cards.back: Hamstring origin

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Ischial tuberosity?
cards.back: Sciatic nerve passes just lateral to it

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Ischial tuberosity?
cards.back: Tender in proximal hamstring tendinopathy (pain on sitting); avulsion injuries in sprinters

cards.front: Where do you find the Patella?
cards.back: The kneecap at the front of the knee

cards.front: How do you palpate the Patella?
cards.back: Knee straight and relaxed; outline its borders and poles — it moves freely when the quadriceps relax

cards.front: What is the Patella a landmark for?
cards.back: Reference for thigh-girth levels (measured above its superior pole)

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Patella?
cards.back: Patellar tendon below, quadriceps tendon above, prepatellar bursa in front

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Patella?
cards.back: Tender inferior pole = patellar tendinopathy ('jumper's knee'); assess mobility and tracking

cards.front: Where do you find the Tibial tuberosity?
cards.back: Bony bump on the front of the tibia just below the knee

cards.front: How do you palpate the Tibial tuberosity?
cards.back: Follow the patellar tendon down from the patella to its bony insertion

cards.front: What is the Tibial tuberosity a landmark for?
cards.back: Patellar tendon insertion; reference for calf girth (10 cm below it)

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Tibial tuberosity?
cards.back: Infrapatellar bursa; Gerdy's tubercle laterally (iliotibial band insertion)

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Tibial tuberosity?
cards.back: Tender and enlarged in active adolescents with Osgood–Schlatter disease

cards.front: Where do you find the Popliteal fossa (popliteal pulse)?
cards.back: Diamond-shaped hollow at the back of the knee

cards.front: How do you palpate the Popliteal fossa (popliteal pulse)?
cards.back: Bend the knee slightly to relax the fascia and press deeply in the centre with both hands

cards.front: What is the Popliteal fossa (popliteal pulse) a landmark for?
cards.back: Popliteal artery pulse — the deepest structure in the fossa

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Popliteal fossa (popliteal pulse)?
cards.back: Tibial nerve (most superficial), popliteal vein, popliteal artery (deepest)

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Popliteal fossa (popliteal pulse)?
cards.back: A swelling here may be a Baker's cyst — but rule out DVT or a popliteal aneurysm

cards.front: Where do you find the Head of the fibula?
cards.back: Bony knob on the outer side of the knee, just below the joint line

cards.front: How do you palpate the Head of the fibula?
cards.back: Follow the biceps femoris tendon down to its bony insertion

cards.front: What is the Head of the fibula a landmark for?
cards.back: Insertion of biceps femoris and the lateral collateral ligament

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Head of the fibula?
cards.back: Common fibular nerve winds around its neck

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Head of the fibula?
cards.back: A blow or tight cast here can cause foot drop (common fibular nerve palsy)

cards.front: Where do you find the Medial malleolus?
cards.back: Bony prominence on the inner side of the ankle

cards.front: How do you palpate the Medial malleolus?
cards.back: Follow the tibia down to the large bump on the inner ankle

cards.front: What is the Medial malleolus a landmark for?
cards.back: End point of leg-length measurement

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Medial malleolus?
cards.back: Tarsal tunnel behind it: tibialis posterior, FDL, posterior tibial artery, tibial nerve, FHL

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Medial malleolus?
cards.back: Feel the posterior tibial pulse behind it; tenderness on its posterior edge counts in the Ottawa ankle rules

cards.front: Where do you find the Lateral malleolus?
cards.back: Bony prominence on the outer side of the ankle — lower and further back than the medial one

cards.front: How do you palpate the Lateral malleolus?
cards.back: Follow the fibula down to its tip on the outer ankle

cards.front: What is the Lateral malleolus a landmark for?
cards.back: Axis for ankle goniometry; the plumb line starts just in front of it

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Lateral malleolus?
cards.back: Anterior talofibular ligament just in front; fibularis tendons behind it

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Lateral malleolus?
cards.back: Bone tenderness at its posterior edge or tip (Ottawa ankle rules) needs an X-ray

cards.front: Where do you find the Dorsalis pedis pulse?
cards.back: Top of the foot, just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon

cards.front: How do you palpate the Dorsalis pedis pulse?
cards.back: Ask the patient to lift the big toe to show the EHL tendon, then feel just lateral to it over the midfoot

cards.front: What is the Dorsalis pedis pulse a landmark for?
cards.back: Pulse check of the foot (and ankle Doppler for ABPI)

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Dorsalis pedis pulse?
cards.back: EHL tendon medially; deep fibular nerve alongside the artery

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Dorsalis pedis pulse?
cards.back: Congenitally absent in some healthy people — always check the posterior tibial pulse too

cards.front: Where do you find the Calcaneus and Achilles insertion?
cards.back: Back of the heel, where the Achilles tendon inserts

cards.front: How do you palpate the Calcaneus and Achilles insertion?
cards.back: Follow the Achilles tendon down to its insertion on the back of the calcaneus

cards.front: What is the Calcaneus and Achilles insertion a landmark for?
cards.back: Achilles insertion; heel alignment (valgus/varus) in posture assessment

cards.front: Which structures lie close to the Calcaneus and Achilles insertion?
cards.back: Retrocalcaneal bursa in front of the tendon; the mid-portion lies 2–6 cm above the insertion

cards.front: Clinical relevance of the Calcaneus and Achilles insertion?
cards.back: Separates insertional from mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy; heel squeeze test for calcaneal stress fracture

cards.front: Before palpating you should…
cards.back: Explain, gain consent and offer a chaperone. Consent and dignity first.

cards.front: The top of the iliac crests is level with…
cards.back: L4. Tuffier's (intercristal) line ≈ L4.

cards.front: The inferior angle of the scapula is level with…
cards.back: T7. Inferior angle ≈ T7.

cards.front: Why compare with the other side?
cards.back: To tell normal tenderness and shape from abnormal. The other side is the patient's own normal.

cards.front: How do you tell C7 from C6?
cards.back: Extend the neck — C6 slides forward and disappears, C7 stays. C7 is the vertebra prominens.

cards.front: Which structure in the popliteal fossa is deepest?
cards.back: Popliteal artery. Nerve superficial, vein, artery deepest.

cards.front: The ischial tuberosity is easiest to palpate with the patient…
cards.back: Side-lying with the hip flexed. Hip flexion moves gluteus maximus off it.

cards.front: From lateral to medial in the femoral triangle:
cards.back: Nerve, artery, vein. NAV(Y) from lateral to medial.

cards.front: Foot drop after a tight below-knee cast suggests compression at…
cards.back: The neck of the fibula. The common fibular nerve winds around the fibular neck.

cards.front: A 13-year-old footballer with a tender, bony lump on the tibial tuberosity most likely has…
cards.back: Osgood–Schlatter disease. Traction apophysitis at the tuberosity in adolescents.

cards.front: Lateral hip pain with tenderness over the greater trochanter, worse lying on that side, suggests…
cards.back: Gluteal tendinopathy (greater trochanteric pain syndrome). Classic GTPS presentation.

cards.front: Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after a fall on an outstretched hand suggests…
cards.back: Scaphoid fracture — immobilise and image. Snuffbox tenderness = scaphoid until proven otherwise.

cards.front: Inversion ankle injury: tender at the tip of the lateral malleolus; walked 4 steps with a limp. — X-ray needed (Ottawa)?
cards.back: Yes — bone tenderness at the malleolar tip. Malleolar bone tenderness alone meets the rule.

cards.front: A 70-year-old with back pain: you feel a pulsatile, expanding mass above the umbilicus. — Action?
cards.back: Urgent medical referral — suspected abdominal aortic aneurysm. Expansile pulsation = AAA red flag.

cards.front: Hot, red, swollen knee, temperature 38.6 °C, can't bear weight; no injury. — Most urgent concern?
cards.back: Septic arthritis — same-day medical referral. Hot joint + fever = septic arthritis until proven otherwise.

cards.front: Neck examination: you count down from C7 and mark 'T6' — your colleague finds T7 on the same patient. — Best interpretation?
cards.back: Palpation of a single spinal level is often one level out — combine landmarks and document. Known limitation; use multiple landmarks and movement.

cards.front: Diabetes: dorsalis pedis not felt on either foot; posterior tibial pulses present. — Interpretation?
cards.back: Can be a normal anatomical variant — but check ABPI given the diabetes. DP can be congenitally absent; diabetes warrants objective testing.

cards.front: Knee injury: 60-year-old, tender only over the patella, can bend to 100°, walked into clinic. — X-ray (Ottawa knee)?
cards.back: Yes — age 55+ and isolated patellar tenderness both meet the rule. Any single criterion triggers imaging.

cards.front: Pain at the medial elbow when gripping; positive Tinel's sign behind the medial epicondyle with tingling into the little finger. — Which structures are involved?
cards.back: Common flexor origin and possibly the ulnar nerve in the cubital tunnel. Medial epicondylalgia can co-exist with ulnar neuropathy.

cards.front: Behind-knee swelling with calf tightness after a long flight; calf 3.5 cm larger. — Before calling it a Baker's cyst you must…
cards.back: Rule out DVT — refer for assessment. Calf swelling after immobility = DVT risk.

cards.front: Insertional heel pain right at the bone, worse with uphill walking; tender at the Achilles insertion, not 4 cm above. — Implication for loading?
cards.back: Insertional tendinopathy — avoid dorsiflexion compression early (e.g. heel drops off a step). Insertional tendons are compressed in dorsiflexion; load flat first.

cards.front: Which finding makes tenderness most clinically meaningful?
cards.back: It reproduces the patient's familiar pain and differs from the other side. Familiar, asymmetric pain — not tenderness alone.
